opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The vision is fairly simple to state but hard to execute: we want to take the enormous amount of data our vehicles already collect — camera, lidar, radar logs from millions of miles of real driving — and turn it into a simulator that is realistic enough that we can trust what happens inside it.

Traditionally, simulators were built by hand. Artists modeled environments, engineers scripted agent behaviors, and you ended up with something that looked reasonable but didn't really match the distribution of the real world. The sensor readings didn't quite look like real sensor readings, and the other drivers and pedestrians didn't behave like real people. That gap matters a lot when you're trying to validate a safety-critical system.

So the idea is to learn the simulator from data. There are really two big pieces. One is sensor simulation: reconstructing scenes from logged data, using neural rendering approaches, so that if the autonomous vehicle decides to do something different than what happened in the log — say it changes lanes or brakes earlier — we can re-render what the cameras and lidar would have seen from that new viewpoint. The second piece is behavior simulation: learning models of how other agents act and react, so when our car deviates from the log, the other cars and pedestrians respond plausibly rather than just replaying their original trajectories blindly.

What makes it scalable is that it's driven by data and learning rather than manual effort. Every mile we drive becomes potential simulation content. We can mine logs for interesting or rare situations, reconstruct them, and then perturb them — add an agent, change timing, make someone more aggressive — to create many variations of difficult scenarios. That lets us test the long tail far more efficiently than waiting for those events to happen on the road.

And ultimately, the measure of success is realism you can quantify. We put a lot of thought into metrics: does the simulated behavior match the statistics of real-world behavior, and does our driver perform in simulation the way it would perform in reality? If you can close that loop, simulation becomes not just a development tool but a core part of how you evaluate and ship a safe driver.

r001.rationale: The response describes reconstructing scenes from logged sensor data and mining rare situations, but it does not clearly state that the environment can be reconstructed for any situation the car encountered.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning behavior models and adding agents to scenarios, but does not identify generative modeling as the way to populate reconstructed environments with additional traffic.

r003.rationale: It says other cars and pedestrians should act and react plausibly when the simulated vehicle deviates from the logged drive.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here.

So the way I think about it is this: we have this fleet of vehicles driving millions of miles in the real world, and every one of those miles is captured with cameras, lidar, radar. That's an incredibly rich record of how the world actually looks and how people actually behave. The question is, how do you turn that record into something you can run forward, something you can perturb and ask "what if" questions of, rather than just replay?

That's really the vision. Instead of hand-building a simulator the way the game industry does, where artists model every building and every pedestrian and you write rules for how cars should behave, you learn the simulator from the data itself. You take the sensor logs and you reconstruct the scene: the geometry, the appearance, the dynamic agents. And then you learn generative models for the parts that have to react, so the other drivers, the pedestrians, the cyclists. Those agents need to behave realistically when our vehicle does something different from what happened in the original log, because otherwise the simulation diverges from reality the moment you change anything.

There are a few pieces that have to come together for that. One is sensor simulation: can you re-render the scene from a new viewpoint so that the camera and lidar inputs look the way they would if the car had actually taken a different path? Neural rendering has made that dramatically more tractable than it was even a few years ago. Another is behavior modeling, which is honestly where a lot of the hard problems live. Human driving is multimodal, it's interactive, and if your simulated agents are too passive or too aggressive you end up training or evaluating against a world that doesn't exist. And then there's the piece around scaling the long tail: taking a real event you've seen once and generating thousands of plausible variations of it, changing the speeds, the geometry, the timing, so you can really stress the system.

The reason this matters so much is that the long tail is where the safety case lives. You can't wait to encounter every rare situation on the road, and you certainly don't want to. But if the simulator is grounded in real sensor data, it inherits the realism of the real world while giving you the controllability of a synthetic environment. That combination is what lets you evaluate and improve at a scale that real-world driving alone could never support.

It's a hard problem, but I think it's one of the key enablers for the whole field. The closer we get to a learned, data-driven simulator that's faithful to the real world, the faster the loop between finding a problem, understanding it, and fixing it becomes.

r001.rationale: The response describes using vehicles’ recorded sensor logs to reconstruct scenes and build a simulator, then scaling real events into many plausible variations.

r002.rationale: It identifies generative models for reactive agents such as other drivers, pedestrians, and cyclists in reconstructed scenes.

r003.rationale: It says those agents must behave realistically when the simulated vehicle takes a different action than in the original log.

astra-6.text:
The vision is to take the data that our vehicles collect and use it to reconstruct a world that we can drive through in simulation. You want more than a replay of what happened. You want to ask, what if the vehicle had taken a different action? What would its sensors have observed, and how would the other road users have responded?

That means bringing together a model of the environment, realistic sensor simulation, and models of how people drive and interact. If you can build those pieces from data, you can turn the variety of situations encountered by a fleet into a much broader set of simulated experiences.

The exciting part is being able to vary those situations and test the driving system under conditions that are difficult to encounter repeatedly on the road. But the simulator also has to be faithful enough that doing better in simulation translates into doing better in the real world. That’s what makes it useful for both developing the system and evaluating it.

r001.rationale: It says vehicle-collected data can reconstruct a world for simulation, but does not clearly state that this works for any situation encountered by a car using that car’s recorded sensor data.

r002.rationale: It does not identify generative modeling as a way to add traffic to reconstructed environments.

r003.rationale: It asks how other road users would respond if the simulated vehicle took a different action, directly stating that their behavior should respond to its decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
The vision is to take the data that our vehicles collect and use it to reconstruct a world that we can drive through in simulation. You want to capture the geometry of the scene, its appearance, and the behavior of the other road users, so that you can put the driving system into that environment and see what it does.

The key is that it has to be more than replaying a recording. If the vehicle takes a different action, the simulation needs to produce the sensor observations it would see from that new position, and the other agents need to respond appropriately. That lets us explore counterfactuals: What if a pedestrian stepped out a little earlier? What if another vehicle behaved differently?

If we can automate that process, every mile we collect becomes a source of simulation scenarios. Then we can test many variations of those scenarios, especially the challenging ones, and use that feedback to improve the system. That's the scalability we're after.
